body: サウジアラビアの首都リヤドにある国際空港が再び攻撃を受け、12人が死亡、300人以上がけがをしました。敵対するイエメンの武装組織フーシ派によるものとみられています。【写真で見る】攻撃された国際空港の現場　サウジアラビア・首都リヤドサウジアラビアの航空当局は10日、首都リヤドの国際空港が攻撃を受け、12人が死亡、309人がけがをしたと発表しました。アメリカのニューヨーク・タイムズは、今回の攻撃による死者数が、2月にアメリカとイスラエルがイランとの戦闘を開始して以降、湾岸諸国で起きた攻撃としては最多だと報じています。ロイター通信によりますと、空港では爆発が起き、出発ゲート付近の天井の一部が崩落したほか、地面に倒れた複数の負傷者が目撃されたということです。運航は一時停止され、航空便の欠航や目的地の変更が相次いでいます。リヤドの空港では今週、イエメンの武装組織フーシ派による攻撃が相次ぎ、これまでに4人が死亡。今回の攻撃について犯行声明は出ていませんが、フーシ派はサウジアラビアが支援するイエメン暫定政権側の軍事攻勢に対抗し、サウジアラビア国内の空港などへの攻撃を強めています。今回の攻撃を受け、アメリカやイギリス、ドイツなどの大使館は、自国民に対し、リヤドの国際空港に近づかないよう呼びかけています。イランをめぐる戦争が周辺国にも波及するなか、サウジアラビアでは民間航空への影響が深刻化していて、地域情勢のさらなる緊迫化が懸念されています。

title: 新聞購読率 初めて5割を下回る
body: 新聞購読率が初めて5割を下回ったことが10日、公益財団法人「新聞通信調査会」（西沢豊理事長）の世論調査で分かった。【ひと目で分かる！】内閣支持率の動くグラフ高市内閣については、米国との外交と物価高への対応で評価が分かれた。調査は7月17日～8月16日、全国の18歳以上の男女5000人を対象に実施し、2676人から回答を得た。今回が19回目。月決めの新聞を購読している人の割合は、昨年度の調査から0．3ポイント減の49．8％だった。調査を始めた2008年度は88．6％で、20年近くで4割強減った。1週間のうちに接するニュースについても、新聞と答えた人は49．7％となり、初めて5割を下回った。民放テレビ（84．2％）、インターネット（74．4％）、NHKテレビ（69．7％）に次ぐ4番手で、ラジオ（27．6％）が続いた。調査では高市内閣に関する質問を初めて追加した。支持率は62．3％で、若年層ほど支持する傾向にあった。政策別では、米外交を50．1％が評価するとした一方、物価高への対応は52．6％が評価しないとした。憲法改正に関心があるとの回答は、65．6％に上った。ただ、賛否は「どちらとも言えない」が5割を占め、改正賛成31．2％、反対15．3％だった。「よいと思う改正内容」（複数回答）は「自衛隊の存在を明記する」が32．6％で最も高かった。

title: 銃殺刑の配信 トランプ氏が判断へ
body:
【ワシントン共同】トランプ米大統領は10日、殺人罪などで死刑判決を受けた元少佐の男の銃殺刑を国防総省が生配信する計画について、配信するかどうかは「最終的に私が決める」と表明した。ホワイトハウスで記者団に語った。超党派の議員から「見せ物にするべきではない」と批判の声が上がっており、世論の反応を見極めるとみられる。【写真】バンス氏「銃殺刑見ない」　生配信計画、超党派で反発
トランプ氏は銃殺刑について「『見せるべきだ』と『見せるな』という二つの意見がある」と指摘。「見せることで、他の人が同じことをしなくなるかもしれない」とも述べ、公開することで抑止効果が期待できるとの考えも示した。男は2009年に米陸軍基地で銃を乱射して13人を殺害したニダル・マリク・ハサン元少佐で、トランプ氏が銃殺刑とすることを承認。事件が起きた南部テキサス州のフォートフッド陸軍基地で12月3日に執行される予定で、ヘグセス国防長官主導で生配信する計画が進んでいる。バンス副大統領は9日、生配信について「私は見るつもりはない」と述べており、政権内でも意見が割れている可能性がある。

title: 障害者50人 9カ月で雇用打ち切り
body:
障害者の働く場を雇用企業に提供する障害者雇用ビジネスの業者を通じ、調剤薬局大手「アインホールディングス（ＨＤ）」（東証プライム、札幌市）の子会社に雇われた障害者約５０人が、会社側の都合により、雇用を９か月で事実上打ち切られていたことが関係者への取材でわかった。障害者は就職前に業者から「１年半のプラン」と説明されており、ショックで働けなくなった人もいた。【図解】一目でわかる…「障害者雇用ビジネス」への新たな規制
約５０人もの障害者が「期間短縮」の上で一斉に退職扱いとなるのは異例だ。この子会社は直接の雇用主であるにもかかわらず「業者から『１年半』とは聞いていなかった」としており、就労管理などを業者任せにする一部の雇用ビジネスのあり方がこうした事態を招いた可能性がある。
この子会社は、全国で「さくら薬局」を展開する「クラフト」（東京都千代田区）。昨年８月にアインＨＤに買収された。
関係者によると、クラフトは同１０月、雇用ビジネス業者「サンクスラボ」（那覇市）の仲介を受け、自社とその子会社で計約５０人の障害者を雇った。障害者らはサンクスラボのオフィスや在宅で勤務した。
障害者らは就職前、サンクスラボから、企業ニーズに合わせて１年半の育成を行う「キャリア開発プラン」と説明されていた。書類上の雇用期間は６か月で、契約更新は「あり得る」、更新上限は「定めなし」などと記載されていた。
ところが、契約更新前の今年３月上旬頃、サンクスラボの担当者から、次の雇用期間は３か月となり、６月末で雇用が終了すると伝えられた。新たな契約書では、次回更新が「なし」に変更されていた。
精神障害のある４０歳代男性は「半年ごとの更新で少なくとも１年半は働けると思っていた」といい、ショックで出勤できなくなり、まもなく退職した。
クラフトは取材に、雇用終了は「障害者と同じ環境で働くという（アインＨＤの）方針が判明したため」とした上で、退職した人の再雇用を検討していることを明らかにした。
サンクスラボは「弊社の契約者とその従業員との契約に関することで、回答を控える」としている。

title: 子供は毎日湯船つかるべき? 解説
body: 「ほぼ1年中シャワーですませている」「お風呂に入る時間もバラバラ」――。毎日の子どもの入浴スタイルについて、「健康のためには湯船に浸かった方がいいのか」と悩む保護者から相談が寄せられました。【写真を見る】子どもは毎日「湯船」に浸かるべき? 小児科医が解説「シャワーでも大丈夫」寝る前の生活リズムNBCラジオ『あさかラ』の「子どもの健康相談室」には、小学3年生の女の子の保護者から次のような相談が寄せられました。【相談内容】小学3年生の娘がいます。ほぼ1年中、子どもも親もシャワーですませることが多いんです。また時間もバラバラです。健康のことを考えたら、やっぱり毎日湯船に浸かった方がいいんでしょうか?この相談に対し、長崎市のやなぎクリニック・栁忠宏先生は、毎日の入浴に対する考え方や湯船に関する研究データ、睡眠につながる生活リズムの整え方について解説しました。■毎日湯船に浸かる必要はある?相談者の「毎日湯船に浸かった方がいいのか」という疑問に対し、栁先生は「結論から言うと、健康のために毎日必ず湯船に浸からなければいけないということはないと思います」と回答しました。栁先生は、「シャワーで汗や汚れをきちんと落としていれば、基本的には大丈夫」と説明。湯船に浸かることは日本人の習慣的な側面が強く、海外では湯船に浸からない国もたくさんあることに触れ、「必ずではないと思います」と話しました。■湯船に関するデータも 中高年の研究と子どもの違い一方で、栁先生は「湯船に浸かると意外といいことも実はデータであったりします」と紹介しました。中高年を対象とした研究では、40度くらいのお湯に10分浸かっていると、入浴している期間はそうでない人に比べて疲労感やストレスなどの自覚的な評価が良かったという報告があるといいます。また、中高年約3万人を長期間追跡した調査では、湯船に浸かっている人の方が心臓や血管の病気が少なかったというデータもあると説明しました。ただし、栁先生は「これは中高年以上の話で、小学校3年生がどうかと言われるとデータがないので、証明されているわけではありません」と補足。「お子さんで湯船に浸かった方がいいというデータはない」としつつも、湯船に浸かる心地よさや、お風呂遊びを通じた親子の思い出になる良さもあると語りました。

title: 米大統領 製油所攻撃巡りウに警告
body: 【AFP＝時事】ドナルド・トランプ米大統領は10日、ウクライナによるロシアの製油所攻撃を強く非難し、ウォロディミル・ゼレンスキー大統領に代わる新たな指導者を選ぶ時期にきていると主張した。【写真】ドローンを発射させるウクライナ兵トランプ氏はホワイトハウスで記者団に対し、ゼレンスキー氏がロシアの製油所を攻撃しないよう求めた自身の指示に従わなかったと語った。米国とイスラエルによるイランとの戦争で世界的な燃料不足が生じており、ウクライナの攻撃がこれを悪化させる恐れがあると指摘。ゼレンスキー氏に対し、ロシアを攻撃してもかまわないが「製油所は攻撃するな」と伝えたことを明らかにし、「絶対にやめるべきだ」と警告した。その上で、ゼレンスキー氏は「何度も取引をまとめることができたはずなのに、なぜかそうしなかった」と述べ、戦争を終結させるために「ウクライナは新しい大統領を迎えるべき時期にきている」と語った。トランプ氏は9日、ロシアが大量の軽油（ディーゼル燃料）を世界市場に供給することで合意したと発表。11月の米中間選挙を前に燃料価格の引き下げを図る狙いで、ロシアに対する制裁を緩和した。ロシアは2022年にウクライナに侵攻して以来、米国やその同盟国などから度重なる制裁を科されてきた。ゼレンスキー氏は、トランプ氏の決定を「パートナーにふさわしくない」「弱腰」だと批判した。ロシア大統領府の経済協力担当特使キリル・ドミトリエフ氏は10日、トランプ氏がウクライナの大統領交代を求めた発言を歓迎した。ドミトリエフ氏はX（旧ツイッター）に「トランプ大統領は、ウクライナにはゼレンスキー氏の好戦的な姿勢ではなく、真に平和を重視する指導者が必要だと考える多くの人々に加わった。象徴的で歴史的だ」と投稿した。一方、欧州連合（EU）のカヤ・カラス外交安全保障上級代表は10日、ロシア産軽油に対する制裁解除は、ロシアによるウクライナ侵攻を助長するだけだと指摘した。カラス氏はSNSに「今はロシアへの圧力を緩める時ではない。欧州は圧力を緩めない」と投稿した。米国とウクライナの関係がぎくしゃくする中、ロシアによるウクライナへの攻撃で、子ども4人を含む少なくとも21人が死亡した。ロシアはここ数か月、ウクライナへの攻撃を激化させており、民間人の死傷者が急増している。一方、4年半以上続く戦争の終結を目指す米国主導の和平交渉は行き詰まったままだ。【翻訳編集】 AFPBB News

title: 米がICC制裁 日本など8カ国反対
body: 外務省は10日未明、米国が国際刑事裁判所（ICC）への制裁を決定したことを受けて、英仏などの7カ国と、ICCの支持を訴える外相共同声明を出した。【写真でみる】赤根所長への制裁に対し集まった17万筆超の署名共同声明ではICCの独立性や公平性への支持を表明し、米国による制裁について「遺憾に思い、強く反対します」と訴えた。制裁が実施された場合は「裁判所の業務、スタッフやその家族に重大な影響を及ぼす」と指摘。ICCやそのスタッフらについて「最も深刻な国際犯罪で訴追された者を裁きにかけ、被害者を支援するために日々尽力している」と言及し「引き続き協力し合い、裁判所の重要な活動を支援し、ルールに基づく国際秩序を守り、責任追及を推進していく」とした。共同声明にはカナダ、デンマーク、ドイツ、フランス、イタリア、オランダ、英国と日本の計8カ国が参加した。

title: 米長官 ICCの「資金源断ちきる」
body:
【ワシントン＝上村健太、ニューヨーク＝大月美佳】米国のトランプ政権は９日、国際刑事裁判所（ＩＣＣ）を制裁対象に指定したと発表した。ルビオ国務長官は声明で「資金源を断ちきる」と表明した。全面的な制裁発動には１８０日間の猶予期間を設け、ＩＣＣ加盟国に対応を求めた。国際社会からは反発の声が相次いでいる。【写真】トランプ氏の不倫相手とされる元ポルノ女優
制裁によって、米国内にあるＩＣＣの資産を凍結し、米国企業とＩＣＣの取引を原則禁じる。米国と取引がある世界中の金融機関がＩＣＣとの取引に二の足を踏むことで、資金調達が滞る可能性がある。
米国はＩＣＣに加盟しておらず、トランプ政権はＩＣＣを「米国の主権に対する脅威」とみなして、これまでも赤根智子所長や判事ら個人に制裁を科してきた。今回、組織としてのＩＣＣを制裁対象としたことで、トランプ政権が目指すＩＣＣの「解体」に向けた圧力を一段と強めた形だ。
ルビオ氏は９日の声明で、ＩＣＣを「ならず者」と断じ、ＩＣＣが米国人を起訴する権限を持つことに長年反対してきたと指摘した。米国の不満は、２０２４年にイスラエルのベンヤミン・ネタニヤフ首相に対する逮捕状をＩＣＣが出したことも背景にある。
ルビオ氏は声明で同盟国に対し、「ＩＣＣを抑制することを期待している」と述べ、同調を求めた。
米国の発表によれば、ＩＣＣの業務維持に必要な一定の取引については、１８０日間の猶予期間が設けられた。米政府は「米国の懸念に対処するため、ＩＣＣ加盟国が外交的・法的な解決に向けて進展を示す期間」としており、各国と対応を協議する可能性がある。
一方、日英独仏やカナダなど８か国の外相は９日、共同声明でＩＣＣへの「揺るぎない支持」を強調した。米国の制裁について「遺憾で、強く反対する」と表明し、ＩＣＣの活動を支援していくとした。
国連のアントニオ・グテレス事務総長も９日、報道官を通じて非難する声明を出し、「ＩＣＣの任務を遂行する能力に与える影響に深い危機感」を示した。
高市首相は９日、トランプ米政権がＩＣＣを制裁対象としたことについて、Ｘ（旧ツイッター）に「我が国は国際社会における法の支配を一貫して重視し、ＩＣＣを支持している。今回の措置は日本の立場と相いれるものではなく、深く懸念している」と投稿した。

title: 米で銃撃 子どもや妊婦ら8人死亡
body: 【ニューヨーク時事】米東部ペンシルベニア州エリー市の住宅街で9日、男（45）が子ども2人を含む8人を銃で殺害した。【写真特集】乱射、銃撃、射殺事件男は犯行後に自殺したとみられる。市当局が10日、明らかにした。記者会見した市警察署長によると、9日午後、銃声検知システムの警報を受けた警官が駆け付け、住宅の前で女性2人が死亡しているのを発見。その後、住宅内で5歳の男の子と1歳の女の子、妊娠中の女性を含む家族6人と容疑者の遺体が見つかった。警察は動機などについて捜査を進める。

約５０人もの障害者が「期間短縮」の上で一斉に退職扱いとなるのは異例だ。この子会社は直接の雇用主であるにもかかわらず「業者から『１年半』とは聞いていなかった」としており、就労管理などを業者任せにする一部の雇用ビジネスのあり方がこうした事態を招いた可能性がある。
この子会社は、全国で「さくら薬局」を展開する「クラフト」（東京都千代田区）。昨年８月にアインＨＤに買収された。
関係者によると、クラフトは同１０月、雇用ビジネス業者「サンクスラボ」（那覇市）の仲介を受け、自社とその子会社で計約５０人の障害者を雇った。障害者らはサンクスラボのオフィスや在宅で勤務した。
障害者らは就職前、サンクスラボから、企業ニーズに合わせて１年半の育成を行う「キャリア開発プラン」と説明されていた。書類上の雇用期間は６か月で、契約更新は「あり得る」、更新上限は「定めなし」などと記載されていた。
ところが、契約更新前の今年３月上旬頃、サンクスラボの担当者から、次の雇用期間は３か月となり、６月末で雇用が終了すると伝えられた。新たな契約書では、次回更新が「なし」に変更されていた。
精神障害のある４０歳代男性は「半年ごとの更新で少なくとも１年半は働けると思っていた」といい、ショックで出勤できなくなり、まもなく退職した。
クラフトは取材に、雇用終了は「障害者と同じ環境で働くという（アインＨＤの）方針が判明したため」とした上で、退職した人の再雇用を検討していることを明らかにした。
サンクスラボは「弊社の契約者とその従業員との契約に関することで、回答を控える」としている。

title: カルテル疑惑 卸売業者が実態証言
body: ビールメーカー大手4社による価格カルテル疑惑をめぐって取引先の卸売業者が取材に応じ、約40年前から卸売業者への販売価格が横並びとなっていた実態について証言しました。ビールメーカー大手4社は、ビールなどについて価格カルテルを結んでいた疑いで強制調査を受けました。10月の酒税改正に合わせ4社から卸売業者に配布された価格表では、各社の数字を見ると、瓶ビール大瓶20本入りで5070円、5071円、5072円と各社似たような価格となっています。4社と取引があった卸売業者の社長は、約40年にわたり、このような実態が続いてきたと話します。4社と取引がある卸売業者:古くから入っている人間としては大手4社の値段（生産者価格）がほぼほぼ変わらない。横一列というのは確かな話。別の卸売業者によりますと、これまでに行われた価格改定の際、各社の営業担当者に対し「カルテルではないか」などと複数回にわたって指摘したこともあったということです。4社が違法性を認識しながら価格調整を続けていた可能性があり、公正取引委員会が調査を進めています。

title: 個人情報漏えい巡る賠償 補償額は
body:
サイバー攻撃による被害が止まりません。大手企業が相次いで個人情報漏えいの恐れがあると発表。■【動画で見る】個人情報が流出した場合企業はどう責任を負うのか？弁護士解説その影響は私たちの生活にも広がりはじめています。異例の事態に国も動き出しています。大切な個人情報が流出した場合、企業にどう責任を問うことができるのでしょうか。元大阪地検検事の亀井正貴弁護士が解説しました。
サイバー攻撃によるシステム障害で授業が休講となっていた大阪公立大学。9日、1週間ぶりにキャンパスには日常が戻ってきました。ただ、教材の共有やメールなど障害が発生したシステムはいまだに利用できない状態で、全面復旧の目途はたっていません。今回のサイバー攻撃で在学生や教職員、受験生など少なくとも13万件の個人情報が流出した恐れがあります。【大阪公立大学に通う学生】「まさか自分が関わっている大学でなる（サイバー攻撃を受ける）と思ってなかったんでめっちゃびっくりしました。学生証の写真が漏えいとか、写真とか使われたら怖い」【大阪公立大学に通う学生】「情報漏洩してないことを祈るばかりです」先月から今月にかけて多くの企業で相次いだサイバー攻撃による被害。
9日、ブックオフでは会員の名前や住所などの個人情報が最大643万件流出した恐れがあることが判明。8日はローソンで215万件以上、カラオケ店を運営する第一興商は約872万件の流出の恐れがあることが明らかになりました。こうした事態を受けて、政府も対策を急いでいます。【高市総理】「政府としては高度化巧妙化する攻撃手法への対策を強化するため、まさに本日、関係省庁による対策会議を実施することとしております」対策会議では、各省庁で情報を収集し、国家サイバー統括室に集約するよう要請。企業に対してはシステムの脆弱性への対策や認証機能の強化、流出した情報の悪用防止などを要請する方針です。
異例の事態に国も動き出す中、生活への影響も出始めています。食品大手ニッスイのグループ会社「日水物流」で7日、不正アクセスが原因とみられるシステム障害が発生。一時、一部の冷凍食品などの入荷や出荷ができない状態となりました。【スーパーことぶき小阪店　中瀬肇店長】「この辺なんか、まるまる。これがずっと入ってこないと大きいと思う」東大阪市のスーパーでは、「日水物流」が扱う冷凍食品が半数近くを占めていて、今の状態が続くと、営業にも影響が出る可能性があります。【スーパーことぶき小阪店　中瀬肇店長】「いまはまだ（在庫が）あるが、今後システム障害が回復しなければ売り場も欠品が起きる。お客さんに迷惑かかって、売り上げが下がるので早いこと解決してほしい」冷凍食品を毎日のように利用する客からは、戸惑いの声も聞かれました。【客】「本当に困ります。家族が多いので重宝している。流通している間にストックしようと。前よりも冷凍食品を買っておくのが多くなったと思う」

title: 「日本一遅い列車」37年歴史に幕
body: JR北海道の釧網（せんもう）線を走る名物観光列車「くしろ湿原ノロッコ号」が10日、運行を終えた。釧路湿原の雄大な景色を、窓からの風を感じながら楽しめると人気を集めたが、車両の老朽化で37年の歴史にピリオドを打った。【写真】釧路川を渡る姿ノロッコは、「トロッコ」と「ノロノロ」を組み合わせた造語。1989年に登場した初代は、貨車を改造してほろをかぶせた開放感あふれる車両を連結。時速30キロほどで走り、「日本一おそ～い列車」と呼ばれた。他の線区でも運行され、道内観光列車の一時代を築いた。釧路市内から最終列車に乗車した田中李奈さん（11）、杏実さん（8）姉妹は「大きな窓から自然の空気を感じられてよかった。動物も見られて、楽しかったので、引退はさみしい」。JR北では、来年から、釧網線や富良野線などで、新しいコンセプトの豪華観光列車「赤い星」「青い星」を走らせる予定。（中沢滋人）

title: プルデンシャル 30年超続いた不正
body:
プルデンシャル生命保険は10月8日、元営業社員などによる金銭詐取問題を巡る調査委員会の報告書を公表した。調査委員会は今回の不正について、一部社員の個人的な問題にとどまらず、成果に連動する報酬制度や、個人の人脈に過度に依存した営業手法などに起因する「構造的かつ経営的な問題」だと厳しく指摘した。得丸社長は自粛の解除について「（現時点で）決定しているものはない」と話す同社は報告書の公表を受け、同日、東京都内で記者会見を開いた。会見には代表取締役社長の得丸博充氏、取締役副社長の秋山泰宏氏、執行役員副社長 兼 営業統括本部長の林邦良氏、最高ガバナンス責任者（CGO）の坂本英之氏が登壇した。会見では、被害に遭った顧客への補償対応、不正を起こした社員への処分、再発防止策の確実な実行の3つを最優先に進めるとした。一方で「抜本的な改革といえるのか」といった記者からの質問に、得丸社長が「再発防止策を実行しただけでは、会社は変われない」と答える場面もあった。約4000人のライフプランナーを抱える生命保険大手プルデンシャル生命保険は、生まれ変わることができるのか。
同社は1月に、社員・元社員100人超が顧客約500人から不適切に金銭を受領していたと発表。不正行為は1991年から2025年まで、30年以上にわたって確認された。さらに、不正の発覚を受けて営業を自粛していた期間中にも、営業社員が複数の顧客に架空の高金利預金を持ちかけ、金銭を受領していた疑いが判明した。社員による顧客情報の無断持ち出しなど、情報漏えい事案も発覚し、ガバナンス上の問題が相次いで明らかになった。報告書によると、被害額は顧客の申告ベースで61億6660万円に上るとしている。また、問題を受けて同社は社員・元社員157人に対し、懲戒解雇などの処分を下した。調査委員会は今回の問題について「一部の営業社員などによる個別の不適切行為ではなく、会社としての構造的な問題」「個人の人脈・人的信頼関係に過度に依存したビジネスが本来の軌道から逸脱した結果」と指摘。経営側の責任にも踏み込んだ。得丸社長は「金銭不祥事などが発生した構造的な要因について、過去の成功体験にとらわれ、社会的要請や環境変化があったにもかかわらず、改革を進めることができなかったと認識している」と述べ、謝罪した。指摘を受け、得丸社長ら現経営陣3人は経営責任を明確にするため、月額報酬の30％を3カ月間、自主返納すると発表。また、過去の経営陣の責任についても、外部専門家による検証を踏まえて明らかにしていく方針を示した。

title: 'Time for Ukraine to get new president,' says Trump after Zelensky condemns diesel deal
summary: Ukraine's leader had said the deal with Russia to release diesel into the US would help Moscow fund the war.
body:
Watch: 'Time for Ukraine to get a new president', says Trump
US President Donald Trump has said he thinks "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president" as he responded to Volodymyr Zelensky's criticism of the US diesel deal with Russia.
The Ukrainian president warned a new deal to release millions of tonnes of Russian diesel into the US would provide Moscow with money to continue its war against his nation, calling it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Trump told reporters outside the White House on Saturday that Zelensky "wants to make problems for the world" by continuing to authorise attacks on Russian refineries.
"He'd better damn well stop," Trump said, before suggesting Ukraine should "get a new leader who can make a deal".
Global fuel supplies, including diesel, have been severely limited by the war against Iran launched by the US and Israel, which led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil products usually flows.
Russia - a major producer - and Ukraine have recently intensified their strikes on each other's energy infrastructure and transport facilities, further straining energy markets.
"We said, 'you can do whatever you want to Russia, don't hit the refineries', because that's a world problem that's caused," Trump continued.
"He could have made many deals and for some reason, he never does."
Putin's envoy Kirill Dmitriev described Trump's intervention as "iconic and historic", saying that Ukraine "needs leadership actually focused on peace".
The US president confirmed on Friday that an agreement had been reached with Moscow to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April.
Zelensky reacted by saying it would allow Moscow to raise new funds to source new military equipment to continue the war.
He also accused Moscow of taking the deal "to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they keep dropping bombs on cities" followingdeadly new strikes on Zaporizhzhia.
Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices
The Ukrainian president spoke to several allies on Saturday to discuss the latest developments, calling for "real decisions to protect lives in Ukraine" and to protect European security.
A Downing Street spokesperson said UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham had spoken to Zelensky and offered his "complete solidarity".
The pair had agreed Russia should acquiesce to "an immediate energy ceasefire" and end its attacks on shipping in the Black Sea, the spokesperson said, as "this would immediately release more energy and food supplies into the global market".
News of the US-Russia diesel deal was also met with criticism by EU's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas, who echoed Zelensky in saying that suspending sanctions "provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war", adding: "This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't."
She said European foreign ministers intended to approve the biggest set of sanctions on Russia since the start of its full-scale invasion on Monday.
The deal with Russia is the latesteffort from Trump to lower fuel prices in the USahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.
That conflict, which began in February, has sent the cost of petrol and in particular diesel skyrocketing, which has soured his standing with the American public who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation.
The average price of diesel is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA – up from last month's $5.94 average, and $3.68 last year.
Under the deal, Russia would release an initial 300,000 tonnes of diesel "to the American and global marketplace" followed by an additional 500,000 tonnes in November.
A further million would follow, Trump wrote on Truth Social, and then another 3m tonnes "within a short period of time" – but he noted that this delivery will be "based on the condition of their diesel refineries".
In the past 10 months, Russia experienced two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country due to Ukrainian drones strikes on its oil refineries.
Diesel production in Russia dropped by an estimated 30%, according to the International Energy Agency.
Trump had alreadycalled for new elections in Ukraine last December,external, saying Ukrainian voters should have the choice to replace Zelensky.
Since the war broke out in 2022 Ukraine has been under martial law, meaning elections are suspended.

title: Twelve killed in attack on airport in Saudi capital Riyadh
summary: Another 309 people are injured, with the Saudi-led coalition saying the attack by Yemen's Houthis is "war crime".
body:
Watch: The scene at Riyadh airport after the strike
At least 12 people have been killed and 309 injured in an attack on an airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, local authorities say, days after Yemen's Houthis claimed similar strikes.
The deaths included four Saudis, two people from Bangladesh and one person each from the US, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, the Saudi civil aviation authority said. Operations at King Khalid International Airport have been suspended.
A Saudi-led military coalition has vowed to respond to the attack, which it has blamed on the Houthis and called a "war crime".
Fighting has recently escalated between Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces and the Houthis, who control most of the country.
On Saturday, a projectile also fell near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam in eastern Saudi Arabia, the Saudi-led coalition said.
The attacks come a day after authorities said three Saudis including a pilot were killed in two attacks on the airport by the Iran-backed Houthis the day prior. Another three people were killed in Houthi attacks on two Saudi airports on 6 and 7 October.
In Saturday's statement, the Saudi civil aviation authority said some of the injured in  were "in critical condition".
It said damage to the airport was being assessed.
An eyewitness who said they had been in the domestic terminal told the news agency that they had seen gate 401 hit and "injured [people] in front of my eyes", adding: "Everyone was running."
More than a dozen ambulances were seen rushing to the airport, according to news agency Reuters, citing an eyewitness.
Saudi-led coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki later said the attack on one of the passenger terminals resulted in deaths and injuries among civilian passengers and airport staff.
He described the attack as a "full-fledged war crime".
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said strongly condemned recent attacks on Saudi Arabia as he confirmed an American citizen was killed in the strikes.
Western embassies in Saudi Arabia have warned their citizens away from the airport. The UK Foreign Office told British nationals to avoid the area "until the airport is secure".
Several Gulf airlines said they had cancelled their flights to and from the airport, with Kuwait Airways citing the "security situation" there.
All flights to Riyadh have either been diverted or cancelled, aviation tracker Flightradar shows.
The Houthis say they are targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war.
The conflict worsened after the Houthis seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive.
That included the port of Mokha on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is the narrowest point of the Red Sea and a chokepoint for global shipping. Yemeni pro-government forces have since said they had "secured" the strait at the southern end of the Red Sea.
A Saudi-led coalition was formed in 2015 after Arab countries joined forces to stop the Houthis taking over Yemen from the country's internationally recognised government.
A temporary ceasefire was brokered in 2022 after years of air strikes and ground fighting led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people, triggering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
But the informal truce began to unravel in July.
The Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
They said they were retaliating against what they described as a years-long Saudi blockade and for an air strike on the airport in Yemen's capital Sanaa, which is controlled by the Houthis.

title: Young men live in fear of being snatched off the streets and sold to Myanmar's army
summary: A desperate junta is in a war of attrition against ethnic militias and and civilian resistance.
body:
Authorities in Myanmar have been ordered to aggressively fulfil the military's recruitment quotas, leading to corruption, extortion and abductions
You do not stay out after dark if you're young and able-bodied in Hpa-An, the capital of Myanmar's southern Karen state. In recent months this has become conventional wisdom.
But Zaw Min has no choice.
"I worry, but I have to go out to work," says the 26-year-old tuk tuk driver, who asked that his real name be omitted out of fear for his safety. "My family call me all the time and remind me not to drive passengers too far; to be careful who I take as a passenger... I have to be vigilant all the time.
"People are panicked and frightened," he explains. "Some people I know have been taken."
Locals say plain-clothed members and supporters of the Myanmar junta have been roaming the streets of Hpa-An, arbitrarily arresting people in their teens, 20s and 30s and forcing them into military service.
According to leaked documents seen by BBC Burmese, authorities have been ordered to aggressively fulfil the military's recruitment quotas across jurisdictions, bolstering the junta's ranks as it endures a war of attrition against ethnic militias, pro-democracy groups and civilian-led resistance movements.
Zaw Min is the only one among his siblings who is at the age of recruitment. Many other "kids" his age have fled, he says – to Thailand, or the homes of relatives further afield. Those who remain are often under strict instructions from their parents: be home before dusk.
Myanmar has been locked in a bloody civil war since February 2021, when its own military launched a coup d'etat and ousted democratically elected leader Aung San Suu Kyi.
Three years later, following a string of humiliating losses, plummeting morale and soaring rates of desertion, the junta enacted a mandatory conscription law that required all men aged 18 to 35 and women aged 18 to 27 to serve at least two years under military command. Those who refuse face up to five years in prison.
The enactment of the law "represents one of the most severe and impactful actions taken against the entire civilian population since the military coup", according to Maj Naung Yoe, military affairs official at the Myanmar Defense and Security Institute (MDSI) and a former military officer who defected and joined the anti-coup Civil Disobedience Movement.
An estimated 100,000 young recruits have been conscriptedby the junta since early 2024
Hpa-An is the latest to be caught in a dragnet that's already ensnared an estimated 100,000 young recruits over the past two-and-a-half years – many of them via coercion, extortion and abductions.
"Security forces track young people's movements to arrest them, force them into service under the pretext of statutory military eligibility, extort money through threats of detention, and arrest individuals during guest-list inspections," Naung Yoe says.
The BBC contacted the Myanmar government's Central Body for Summoning People's Military Servants regarding incidents mentioned in this story, including the forced recruitment of conscripts and reports of abductions allegedly carried out in recent months.
They said they had no comment on the matter.
With the mandatory conscription law, the junta has established a human supply chain to sustain its armed forces. And it appears to have worked. Observers note that reinforcements have played a critical role in helping the regime claw back more territory. In many parts of Myanmar, the resistance is now on the back foot.
The war, though, is far from over. And as more youths evade conscription – either to join the resistance or simply avoid armed conflict against their fellow countrymen – the junta's recruitment methods have become ever more extreme.
International rights groups such as Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and Fortify Rights say Myanmar's military is abducting civilians and forcing them into military service.
In July, open-source research organisation Myanmar Witness revealed that they had analysed hundreds of missing-person advertisements collected from Facebook between 2021 and 2025.
Researchers found that missing person notices for January rose from four in 2021, pre-coup, to 82 in 2025, post-conscription law.
"In practice, much of [the Myanmar military's] recruitment appears to be carried out through detention, coercion, and disappearance rather than formal call-up, and often without notice to families," they concluded.
Men and boys constituted the majority of reported missing persons.
Watch: BBC goes into jungle with Myanmar's civil war rebels
"They are spreading rumours all over the neighbourhood that I sold my husband."
Ma Moe San Pan sobs the words through gulps of air. She is sitting in her kitchen, at home in Yangon, where on the morning of 8 May 2025 she saw her 33-year-old husband Phyo Wai for the last time.
"We had an argument, and afterwards he left home," she recalls."I was upset and told my cousin about what had happened."
Ma Moe San Pan's cousin worked at the local ward administration office, and she asked him to bring her husband back. It was two days later that Phyo Wai called her, from a military recruitment centre on the other side of the city.
The cousin had taken him to the ward office which had sold him on to another ward for 4 million kyats ($900; £680) to fill that ward's recruitment quota, Ma Moe San Pan says. The BBC was unable to reach Ma Moe San Pan's cousin.
In a desperate attempt to bring him back, Ma Moe San Pan was then scammed out of 4.5 million kyats by strangers who falsely promised his release.
U Maung Maung Lwin, the administrator of the ward to which Phyo Wai was taken, later admitted to the BBC that he had played a role in sending him to the military recruitment authorities.
When asked about allegations that individuals were being conscripted outside their home township, he said transfers from other townships do occur when local quotas cannot be met.
But he denied that any money was involved in such cases, or in Phyo Wai's forced conscription.
"[Phyo Wai] told me they said they would help him and made him sign documents," Ma Moe San Pan recalls.
"If my husband had been legally selected for conscription through the normal process, I could have accepted that. What I cannot accept is that our own ward administration office allegedly sold him to another ward.
"I also regret placing my trust in my cousin."
Ma Moe San Pan says her husband was sold into military service by her own cousin
In the time since Phyo Wai was taken, Ma Moe San Pan has filed police complaints relating to two matters: the sale of her husband into military service, and the 4.5 million kyats she lost to scammers.
The police accepted her complaint, she says, but refused her request to include human trafficking charges, claiming a human trafficking case could only be registered if a person had been sold abroad.
She does not know where her husband is now.
Ma Moe San Pan's case highlights a grim mutation of the junta's mandatory conscription laws: mounting pressure from the higher levels of the regime has created perverse incentives further down the chain of command.
Surging demand and dwindling supply have fuelled an illicit market for eligible recruits. And with money on the table, security officials have taken to arresting youth at road checkpoints, tracking and ambushing workers during their daily commutes, setting traps via fake job advertisements, and forcibly entering people's homes, Naung Yoe says.
"Under the guise of the conscription law, these coercive arrests and recruitment drives have effectively transformed into a modern-day slavery and human trafficking enterprise."
In late August, police in Yangon arrested a member of the Fire Services Department – a branch of the home affairs ministry – and his son-in-law for abducting four young men with the intention of selling them for military conscription.
The reserve fire brigade unit commander allegedly deceived the men with promises of employment opportunities, luring them to his house and trapping them in a series of purpose-built detention rooms. Police officers raided the residence and arrested him on 25 August. He has since been charged with kidnapping or abducting in order to wrongfully confine a person, and faces up to 7 years in prison.
BBC Burmese made several attempts to contact the police station where he is being held, but was unsuccessful.
"Lower-level administrative bodies, military personnel and local criminal gangs employ diverse tactics to press-gang and arrest young people," Naung Yoe says.
"They sell these individuals to military units and regional commands facing manpower shortages, or traffic substitute recruits on behalf of wealthier individuals seeking to buy their way out of service."
It's been more than a year since Ma Moe San Pan last saw her husband Phyo Wai
While conscription orders are indiscriminate on paper – demanding a quota of recruits from each village, ward, or township proportional to its population – wealthier conscripts can simply pay to dodge the draft and be replaced by someone more financially vulnerable.
So it is the poor who disproportionately bear the burden.
Naung Yoe, meanwhile, told the BBC that "these practices are escalating due to increasing difficulties in meeting monthly recruitment quotas and the lucrative financial profits made from recruit trading at the ground level".
But the hardening fist of forced conscription also reveals the junta's empty hand, and its desperation for manpower.
It "seems to be another step in the junta's efforts to enlist unwilling youth in a conflict that underscores its embattled position in the civil war" says Dr Sandeep Singh, a research fellow who teaches military studies at the National University of Singapore.
The climate surrounding routine abductions, he adds, has "generated further difficulties on the youth of Myanmar, already affected by years of civil war, and their families".

title: Russian glide bomb attack on Zaporizhzhia kills at least 20 people
summary: Volodymyr Zelensky says the attack, which left children dead, was Russia expressing its "thanks" for a US diesel deal.
body:
A number of people are believed to be still under the rubble of the destroyed apartment building in Zaporizhzhia
Russia has attacked the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia with five glide bombs, killing at least 20 people including four children, local officials said.
The glide bombs hit residential buildings in the southern city on Saturday morning. At least32 others were injured in the attack, with more still missing and believed to be under the rubble.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attacks on Zaporizhzhia were Russia expressing "its thanks" for a deal announced by US President Donald Trump last night easing sanctions on Moscow to import Russian diesel.
He added that 13 other regions had come under attack overnight, arguing this demonstrated Russia took "any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting".
Photos and videos from the site of one of the strikes in Zaporizhzhia show an apartment block mostly destroyed.
"The ground floor was hit, and the floors above just collapsed," acting Mayor Regina Harchenko told Ukrainian television from the scene.
She said more than 80 workers were involved in ongoing search and rescue operations which are expected to continue throughout the day.
The rescuers regularly stop to listen for any noises made by survivors who could be under the rubble.
Harchenko said Russia had struck at "our very heart" and "our littlest ones" were among those killed, adding that their deaths were "awful grief for their families. For the city."
Zaporizhzhia is a major regional centre with more than 700,000 residents. It is located less than 10 miles (16km) from the front lineand is frequently attacked by Russian drones and missiles.
Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky calls it a gift to Putin
Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices
Zelensky was quick to criticise Trump's diesel deal with Russia, calling ita gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin. Analysts view the deal as an attempt by the US president to allay domestic concerns about high fuel prices ahead of the upcoming midterm elections.
Zelensky wrote on social media on Saturday that Russian attacks on energy facilities in the capital, Kyiv, demonstrated Russia's "true intentions".
"Russia's choice is war. And they will be ready to end it only when they feel that their ability to drag the war out is diminishing.
"Unfortunately, the signals Russia received yesterday were entirely different – signals suggesting that it could simply keep attacking. And this needs to be corrected."
Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months, as Moscow's full-scale invasion, launched in 2022, drags on.
On Thursday, at least 33 people were killed in another Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in Kramatorsk, in the eastern Donetsk region.
The day before,22 people including five childrendied as a Russian missile hit an apartment block in the town of Pryluky, east of Kyiv.
The number of civilian casualties in Ukrainejumped by 55%,externalin the first eight months of this year, according to the UN.
Russia hasalso stepped up its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructureas winter approaches, a strategy it has undertaken in previous years. Kyiv has repeatedly accused it of targeting Ukraine's civilian population, which Moscow denies.
For its part, Ukraine has increasingly adopted a policy of striking infrastructure often deep inside Russia that is crucial to its economy, including several oil refineries and terminals.
Severalstrikes on data centres owned by Yandexhave left the tech giant struggling to maintain services.
Kyiv says its strikes are aimed at curtailing revenue streams for Russia's war machine.

title: US murderer Christa Pike discharged from hospital 10 days after failed execution
summary: Pike's lawyers say she is "grateful" to the medical team who cared for her after she survived two lethal injections last month.
body:
US death row inmate Christa Pike has been discharged from hospital following her botched execution at the end of last month, her lawyers have said.
Pike, 50, has been sent back to the prison where she has spent the last 30 years and is continuing to receive medical care, according to a statement from her lawyers on Saturday.
She survived two lethal injections of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September, which left her in a critical condition.
Pike regained consciousness earlier this week and began speaking - stunning experts, medical staff and her lawyers.
Her case is now in uncharted territory as she is thought to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.
I've seen nearly 500 executions - but never one like Christa Pike's
I interviewed Christa Pike 20 years ago - I can't stop thinking about her
What happened in Christa Pike's failed US execution, and how did she survive?
Pike's lawyers said in their statement that she was "grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances".
It is unclear what medical care Pike is receiving now that she is back in prison but her lawyers previously said she faced a "long road to recovery".
The Tennessee Department of Correction is yet to say why the execution did not go as planned, though it has defended the method it used.
How widely used is the death penalty in the US?
At a court hearing on Wednesday, Tennessee Assistant Attorney General Will Ayers told the judge he did not know whether the state intends to try to execute her again.
The judge ordered the state to preserve all evidence related to the failed injections. That evidence could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.
Shipp was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison.
Pike was the first woman scheduled to be executed in the state of Tennessee in over 200 years.
Her lawyers have spent decades appealing her case. In the days leading up to her scheduled execution, both the US Supreme Court and Tennessee Governor Bill Lee declined to block the execution.
Since it failed, Pike's lawyers have renewed their calls for her sentence to be commuted to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed by Pike and Shipp
Pike lost consciousness and was taken to a local hospital following her botched execution. Her legal team believed for days that she was brain dead and expected her to be taken off life support at any moment.
Pike eventually woke up and began talking again on Tuesday - her lawyer Randy Spivey said her first words were "Where am I?" and "Who are you?"
At a press conference on Wednesday, her lawyers said she was shackled to the bed and suffering from pneumonia and significant swelling on her arms, while also being unable to swallow.
"We don't know the toll all of this will take" Spivey said of her mental health, adding that Pike felt "angry and confused".

title: Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky calls it a gift to Putin
summary: Ukraine's president sharply criticised the move, calling it an "investment in war that must be ended, not prolonged".
body:
Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met in Alaska last year
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has condemned Donald Trump's announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel into the US.
Zelensky called it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged", a position quickly backed by Ukraine's European allies.
Trump said Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and another million after that.
It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen.
Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform that a further three million tonnes of Russian diesel would be delivered "within a short period", dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine.
Putin later said Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, was willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products,but his statement did not specify amounts.
Zelensky said Russia would repay the diesel with "further terror".
"We count on America's fair support for our defence of life, for our defence of people in Ukraine – and on the United States having a correspondingly strong conversation with Russia. A strong one, not a weak one," he wrote.
He laterpointed to deadly overnight strikes on Zaporizhzhia and Kyivas Russia expressing "its thanks" for the agreement.
Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers.
Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices
Russian glide bomb attack on Zaporizhzhia kills at least 15 people
Tim Armitage, an investment strategist at Quilter Cheviot, said the numbers mentioned by Trump were "relatively small".
He said the first tranche equated to approximately 2.25 million barrels, and daily US consumption was around 3.8 million barrels, "so it won't make a material difference to pump prices in the US".
"Granted, there are then two more releases to come, but it does appear to be a slightly desperate move by President Trump to try to lower inflation ahead of the midterms."
The BBC has asked the White House what Russia will get from the US in return for the commitment.
The agreement with Russia also opens Trump up to criticism from European allies and pro-Ukraine politicians in the US that the American president is now helping to fund Moscow's war machine.
The EU's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said suspending sanctions "provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war", adding: "This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't."
She said European foreign ministers intended to approve the biggest set of sanctions on Russia since the start of its full-scale invasion on Monday.
Meanwhile, a UK government spokesperson said its position "could not be clearer" and that it would continue working with international partners to support Ukraine and bring about sustained peace.
"We will also maintain pressure on Russia through the toughest sanctions regime ever imposed by the UK, increasing the cost of Putin's aggression and supporting efforts to secure a just and lasting peace."
Friday's announcement is the latest effort from Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.
That conflict, which began in February, has sent the cost of petrol and in particular diesel skyrocketing, which has soured his standing with the American public who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation.
Ukraine's President Volodymr Zelensky said Russia would repay the diesel with "further terror"
The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September.
Shortly after Trump's announcement, the US Treasury formally issued a temporary licence allowing Russian diesel into the market.
Putin said he had spoken to Trump about the global energy situation on Friday, adding: "The Russian side confirmed its willingness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US market and global markets at large."
An envoy for Putin, Kirill Dmitriev, welcomed the deal on social media, saying: "Russia-US co-operation on diesel and energy will benefit the world."
Russia has this year experienced two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries. Its diesel production has fallen by nearly 30%, according to International Energy Agency estimates.
Trump has expressed his displeasure over those attacks, blaming them for rising fuel prices.
But Zelensky defended the strikes on Friday, saying they were in response to "Russia's years-long campaign of terror against Ukraine's energy sector".
"Ukraine will not set Russian oil refineries on fire if Russia does not destroy our energy infrastructure," he said.
Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work?
Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information, and the details of exactly how Russia will supply this fuel to the global market is unclear.
But the announced deal represents a remarkable about-face, as the US Congress recently enacted legislation - signed by the president - to authorise new American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.
What impact the deal with Russia will have on fuel prices also remains unclear. The global benchmark for crude oil, Brent, remains above $103 a barrel. Before the war with Iran, Brent crude was trading at about $73 a barrel.
With the looming US elections - which will determine whether Republicans maintain control of Congress - Trump has been searching for ways to ease his Republican party's political pain.
Earlier this week, he said he was "thinking about" suspending the federal tax on gasoline and also announced that he would allow so-called red dye diesel to be used on US highways without facing federal tax.
Trump has also successfully pressured G7 nations into releasing 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from stockpiles to help ease supply concerns and previously supported calls for a ban on diesel exports from the US.

title: Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices
summary: The US president hopes to ease his party's pain before next month's midterm elections, writes the BBC's North America correspondent.
body:
Donald Trump's decision to import Russian fuel to the US represents a remarkable about-face from the president.
Just three weeks ago, Trump signed legislation to authorise fresh American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.
Now, Trump says, Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the US and world markets in the coming months.
The deal comes as Trump is still grappling with the political fallout of the Iran war and its impact on global energy prices, weeks before American voters head to the polls in the midterm elections.
As the cost of fuel has skyrocketed in America, his standing with the public – stung by the higher prices at the pump and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation – has soured.
The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.
It is these states – places like Iowa, Kansas, Texas and Ohio – that have become unexpected political battlegrounds in the upcoming elections that will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress.
Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky criticises 'gift to Putin'
What are the US midterms? A simple guide
For months, the American president has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.
Herecently pressured European allies to further tap their oil reserves. He deferred federal taxes on the fuel and authorised supplies designated for farm use to be used in interstate trucking.
He has also promised that he would not renew attacks on Iran until after the midterms – an unusually frank acknowledgement of the political impact the ongoing conflict is having.
His decision to strike a deal with Russia's Putin is only the latest, most dramatic effort.
Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information, of course. The details of exactly how Russia is supplying this fuel to the global market, and what they might get for in return – besides much-needed hard currency – is unclear.
It opens Trump to criticism from European allies and American politicians that his administration is now helping to fund the Russian war machine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal a "gift" to Putin that Russia would "repay" with "terror and perfidy".
"Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he wrote on X.
It is also uncertain exactly how much Trump's move will help Republicans at the ballot box.
The promised European diesel release hasn't moved energy prices significantly, and there's no information on the speed with which Russian fuel could enter the market.
Its diesel refinery capacity has been damaged by repeated Ukrainian strikes – attacks that Trump has encouraged Zelensky to curtail.
The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tons this month, that amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.
Americans may not notice much of an immediate difference.
With less than a month before November's midterm elections, early voting has already started in many states. The political cake, as the saying goes, is all but baked.
"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in his Truth Social post.
But over the past seven months, prices on energy, fuel and consumer goods have only gone up - even as Trump and his officials have repeatedly assured an uneasy public a successful resolution to the war, and an easing of its economic impact, is nearly at hand.
Trump may be left hoping that his latest deal, setting aside its potentially uncomfortable diplomatic issues, will be enough to convince American voters that his promise of impending economic relief is more than just empty words.

title: Boots has a new owner: Three ways it could affect you
summary: The stalwart of Britain's High Street has been sold to a Canadian billionaire family. What will that mean for you?
body:
If you have been looking to buy a health or beauty product, the chances are you will have shopped at a Boots somewhere in the UK.
The pharmacy and retailer is a stalwart of Britain's high streets, where it has served generations of customers for decades.
But now it is set to enter its 178th year under new ownership after an £7bn deal was agreed this week - here's three ways it could affect your shopping experience.
Upgrading its portfolio of 1,800 stores is high on the list of Boots' new owners, Wittington Investments. This is the holding company of the Westons -  a wealthy and retail-steeped Canadian family who used to own Selfridges and currently own several large retailers across the Atlantic.
The UK branch of the family also controls the owner of Primark, Associated British Foods (ABF).
What Boots stores might look like in the future has not been disclosed.
Business has been good for Boots in recent years, and new-look beauty areas in some of its bigger shops have given shoppers more of a department store experience, according to Sofie Willmott, an associate director and analyst at GlobalData Retail.
Since the opening of its first beauty-only store in 2023 in the Battersea Power Station development, it says it has redesigned over 180 beauty halls, while also opening its first fragrance concept store and an Opticians dedicated to luxury eyewear.
"They should invest in the rest of the chain because they've got such a big store portfolio that I think some of the smaller stores have really lacked investment over time, and I think that is something that they need to kind of catch up with," Willmott says.
A more "consistent" look would also be an improvement, Willmott adds. "At the moment there is a bit of a disconnect."
Jackie Naghten, a retail industry veteran who has worked for the likes of Top Shop, Marks & Spencer and Debenhams, thinks Boots' stores need to be made "more functional" by not having their health hubs "squeezed in the corner".
But Yasmin Trimble, 22, who buys beauty products from Boots, likes how easy the stores are to navigate.
"You can get everything you need...it is not confusing. It has got a cleaner aesthetic to it as well."
Katie Burrows and Yasmin Trimble both shop at Boots regularly
Boots was an early adopter of the loyalty cards commonly offered today by companies offering points and discounts to customers who sign up.
Its Advantage card, launched in 1997, is unlikely to go away and remains popular.
Naghten doesn't think they would get rid of it. "It's the best-value store card in terms of bang for your buck."
The card offers shoppers three points for every pound they spend. Each point is worth 1p.
Katie Burrows, 23, is a fan of building up the points to get money off.
She mainly shops at Boots for skincare, first aid and medicine, but thinks prices for its sanitary products are "ridiculously expensive" - something her friend Yasmin agrees with.
Lewis Harrison believes the loyalty card is also good value, but finds it "frustrating how the rewards points only cover a full transaction".
"I wish you could use your points for a partial transaction like you can in Holland and Barrett," the 25-year-old says. "It would be good to use the points towards more expensive transactions."
Natalie Berg, retail expert and founder of consultancy NBK Retail, suggests the Advantage card gives Boots "a unique understanding of their customers" and is an asset the new owners "will want to double down on".
"As AI and social media change how people discover and buy products, that direct relationship with customers will only become more important."
The new owners have already signalled they plan to expand Boots' healthcare service, a booming industry at the moment.
The retailer started out as an apothecary, so health is in its roots. Today, it offers a wide range of health and wellbeing services as well as prescriptions and vaccinations through its in-store pharmacies.
It also announced earlier this summer it was expanding services for weight loss drugs, which have surged in popularity.
Naghten points out that the Weston family's purchase of Boots comes at a time when pharmacies areincreasingly going to prescribe more medications and health services, in a bid to ease pressure on GP surgeries and hospitals.
"They didn't buy this thing for no reason. They have got the blueprint," she says.
While health will remain a core part of its business, Boots has other strengths, Naghten adds, in its No7 make-up and skincare products.
"When you have all these people coming in for health and wellbeing services, they will also be picking up a lipstick," she says.
Willmott suggests Boots has an "edge" over its rivals on the health side, given its reputation as an expert.
But the company is facing tough competition, which Boots acknowledged affected revenues in its latest financial results.
Shoppers, particularly younger ones, are increasingly seeking products online through influencer ads rather than heading to brick-and-mortar shops.
There are also other big players, such as Superdrug. And M&S this week announced a new partnership with Sephora, saying it would replace a hundred of its own beauty departments with the brand next year.
For 18-year-old Schekina Bourne, Boots is not a "go-to shop" for her. "Even though I can go to Boots even in my area....Superdrug is like closest to me. So, I'll prefer the convenience," she says.

title: Burnham promises to curb non-compete rules in job contracts
summary: The prime minister says restrictions on what workers can do after leaving roles have "gone too far".
body:
Andy Burnham has promised to curb companies' ability to restrict what their workers can do after leaving their job.
In a speech, the prime minister said the use of non-compete clauses in employment contracts had "gone too far" and was holding innovative UK companies back.
He added the clauses had forced workers to go without pay after leaving a role, as well as making it harder for growing firms to hire new staff.
Ahead of the Budget later this month, he also said there was "more to do" on tax to encourage promising firms to stay in the UK.
Sir Keir Starmer's government had been exploring possible restrictions on non-compete clauses since late last year, including a total ban, banning them above a certain salary threshold, or limiting how long they can last.
Although commonly associated with the financial services and technology sectors, research cited by the government has estimated around 5 million jobs in Britain are covered by the clauses, typically lasting around six months.
Speaking at a business summit in Manchester, Burnham confirmed his government would press ahead with new legislation to ensure the clauses can "no longer be a barrier" to hiring new staff.
He added that their use had stopped workers leaving to join other companies, or founding their own firms instead, adding: "I think that's a drag on innovation."
Referencing alandmark 1995 court rulingthat is credited with revolutionising the football transfer market in Europe, he said he hoped reining in non-compete clauses could prove the "Bosman ruling for the innovation sector".
Burnham did not specify the scope of the restrictions he is planning, but suggested they would apply to the "everyday economy" as well as helping "promising start-ups and scaling firms".
It is understood that the government is planning to unveil details of the proposed restrictions, which were first reported byPolitico,externalandThe Financial Times,external, alongside the Budget on 28 October.
Responding to the prime minister's comments, the Recruitment and Employment Confederation warned against "sweeping" changes to non-compete rules, adding they played a "vital role" in protecting commercially sensitive information and client relationships.
The previous Conservative government hadruled out a total ban,externalon non-compete clauses, after hearing from employers that it could reduce investor confidence in the UK or prompt companies to tighten how they share information internally.
The prime minister sought to frame the announcement on non-compete clauses as part of a wider government pitch to boost innovative sectors of the economy.
He told the summit that although the UK was home to outstanding research and start-ups, too many companies had gone abroad in search of investment.
He also signalled that the government would "say more" at the Budget about plans to use public investment as a way to encourage private funding in the economy.
He added that he wanted all UK regions to have a dedicated fund to do this, modelled on the Good Growth Fundlaunchedin Greater Manchester last year, during his tenure as mayor of the city-region.
He also hinted that the government was looking at the tax system to ensure the UK can retain high-growth companies.
He said: "One of our biggest challenges is breaking through our own ceiling. Too often, our best ideas are developed and scaled overseas, and with it the jobs, technology and investment that goes with them."
"So I know there is more to do to fix that, specifically on tax, to encourage people to stay and scale."

title: Ex-Deutsche Bank trader jailed for rigging rates has conviction overturned
summary: The Court of Appeal quashes the conviction of Christian Bittar, a former Deutsche Bank trader jailed in 2018.
body:
Christian Bittar, left, and his wife Caroline
Another former banker sentenced in one of the biggest scandals of the financial crisis has had his conviction overturned following a long-running legal battle.
The Court of Appeal has quashed the conviction of Christian Bittar, a former Deutsche Bank trader who went to prison in 2018 for "manipulating" the benchmark interest rate, Euribor.
It comes after the same UK court overturned five convictions of ex-Barclays bankers in the rate rigging trials earlier this week.
Bittar, who watched proceedings via video link from Switzerland because he was not granted a visa to attend court, told the BBC: "I have waited a very, very long time for this day."
The financial crisis began in 2008, sending huge economic shockwaves across the world and triggering recessions in many countries.
There was a public backlash against bankers, held by many to be responsible for the crisis, while the financial sector was protected by taxpayer-funded bailouts.
The Libor scandal erupted in 2012, when it was discovered that at the outbreak of the financial crisis, banks had been misrepresenting their positions during the process of setting the lending rate, helping to boost profits and mask difficulties.
Some 19 City traders were convicted in the US and UK between 2015 and 2019 across nine criminal trials held in London and New York.
Eighteen of these have now been acquitted.
Only one former trader in the world now remains convicted: former Barclays trader Peter Johnson, who was also one of the original whistleblowers in the interest rate rigging scandal. He pleaded guilty on advice that he had little chance at winning at trial. The court confirmed that he too has now applied to appeal against his conviction.
The news has already prompted lawyers and senior politicians to press for the Bank of England and the Treasury to release all their records about their own roles in interest rate 'rigging' during the financial crisis, amid concerns raised of a cover-up of the role of central banks and governments.
Speaking after his conviction was quashed, Bittar said: "Finally the injustice of what I and others suffered has been recognised.
"I am so grateful for those who stood by me through this ordeal and those who worked so tirelessly to correct it."
His wife, Caroline, who lives in the UK, said their family had lost 15 "valuable years", with their children "growing up with this injustice".
She added they were looking forward to "enjoying life with our family and friends without this shadow hanging over us".
On Wednesday, Jay Merchant, Jonathan Mathew, Alex Pabon, Colin Bermingham and Philippe Moryoussef saw their convictions for 'manipulating' the interest rate benchmarks Libor and Euribor quashed after a 10-year struggle for justice.
Philippe Moryoussef, acquitted this week and his wife, Karine Moryoussef
They launched fresh appeals against their jail sentences following a Supreme Court ruling last year that acquitted Tom Hayes, the first to be jailed for 'rigging' interest rates in 2015, and Carlo Palombo, jailed in 2019.
Tom Hayes, who was initially sentenced to 14 years, reduced on appeal to 11, is now seeking damages from his former employer UBS.
The traders were among 37 City traders and brokers prosecuted for "manipulating" the interest rate benchmarks Libor and Euribor, which track the cost of borrowing cash between the banks and have been used to set the interest rates on millions of mortgages and commercial loans.
The BBC has uncovered evidence of a much larger, state-led 'rigging' of interest rates, under pressure from central banks and governments across the world. Evidence implicating Downing Street and the Bank of England was suppressed throughout the criminal trials.
Former Conservative cabinet minister David Davis told the BBC the innocent traders had been the victims of a series of miscarriages of justice.
He said the people exonerated this week and before were "the victims of a scapegoating exercise which arose as a result of the government's own misbehaviour in lowballing [falsely understating] Libor interest rates themselves, in order to try and rescue the economy after their own self-induced crash in the late 2000s".
In 2015, during the first trial for interest rate 'rigging', of former UBS trader Hayes, Mr Justice Jeremy Cooke decided as a matter of law that any attempt to influence the rates could not be lawful, and that any rate influenced by commercial interest must automatically be false. Judges in the subsequent eight trials followed suit.
However, in July 2025, the Supreme Court decided that all the judges had erred, misdirecting juries that it was wrong as a matter of law. Instead, whether the requests were right or wrong was properly a matter of fact for the jury to decide, not the judge.
All convictions in the United States were overturned in 2022 after an appeal court ruled that there was insufficient evidence that the traders' requests had broken any rules or laws.

title: Green Party MP wants to make sure it is 'not vulnerable to extremists'
summary: The party's Westminster leader Ellie Chowns made the comments after ex-leader Caroline Lucas said some members had joined to vote in the Zionism motion.
body:
Green MP Ellie Chowns leads the party in the Commons, where it has five MPs
A Green Party MP has said her party needs to make sure it is not "vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists" after members voted for a motion that claimed Zionism was racism.
The motion put forward by activists, which became formal policy after it was approved at the Green's conference earlier this month, has divided senior party figures and been criticised by Jewish groups.
Westminster leader Ellie Chowns told the BBC it was a "significant and damaging policy" and she would work to reform the Green Party.
It comes after ex-leader Caroline Lucas said it was not being protected from entryism - where people sign up to a party to try to change it.
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today Programme on Saturday, Chowns said: "I don't know if there are extremists and racists in my party. But I want to make sure that my party isn't vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists."
The MP described Zionism as a "contested concept" and said the motion did not represent the views of the large majority of Green Party members, "nor of people in the country".
Chowns said the motion would be a "distraction from the very important work" the party has been doing campaigning for Palestinian rights.
She added: "I think it is clear that if we have policy, such significant and damaging policy, made by a vote of just 0.4% of our members, that something isn't working in our structures and our policy-making process."
Members of the Green Party of England and Wales endorsed the policy motion by 1,022 votes to 813.
There are 230,000 members of the Green party overall and not everyone attended the conference.
The policy also backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.
It defines Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state".
The Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council, which criticised the motion, said: "Zionism is anti-racism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it."
Caroline Lucas was the Green Party' first and sole MP until 2024
Appearing on BBC Radio 4 programme Any Questions on Friday, Lucas said she was not putting any blame on the party's current leader, Zack Polanski, who she said had done "great things" for the party.
"Our constitution was written decades ago, well before we had MPs, before we had mayors, before we had anything like the number of that we have today," the ex-leader said.
Lucas, who was for years the face of the Greens as its first and sole MP until 2024, added the party needed to be made "a welcoming place for Jewish people."
A Green Party spokesperson said: "Green Party membership has increased since Zack Polanksi announced his leadership bid in May 2025. Unlike other political parties, our members can bring and set policy.
"This is one motion alongside dozens of others that was discussed at our biggest-ever party conference. Every motion submitted to conference undergoes debate and no single interest group drives policy. "
Polanski, who is Jewish, previously told the BBC he would not have voted for the motion and instead would have voted for an amended version.
However, he said the "substantial part of the motion", that "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by a racist ideology" was "obvious".
Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.
Ashok Kumar, a Green Party member and part of the Greens for Palestine group, voted for the motion and told the BBC last week it was about "Palestinian liberation."
He said he didn't feel the vote was harming the image of the Green Party, and that a growing number of people see this as a core issue.
"They see the violence that's (been) occurring over the last three years,"he told BBC Politics Live.,external"So, I think the Zionist position is actually the marginal position.
The Greens have had a surge in support after Polanski took over as leader in September last year but in recent months polls suggest this has waned
Following Polanksi's by-election defeat in Holborn and St Pancras this week,the leader of the Jewish Greens Vivien Lichtenstein said he should resign.
She added it was a "big mistake" for him to have dodged a debate about a party conference motion that declared Zionism a form of racism.
Polanski did not stay at conference to vote on the motion or amendments. He left early to campaign for the north London by-election, which Labour won on Thursday with Greens coming second.
Following his defeat, Polanski told BBC Breakfast he would "absolutely" stay on as leader and he "of course" had not questioned that.
He lost out to Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali - who secured 45% of the vote to his 33% - but the Green vote share was up by 22 percentage points on the 2024 general election.

title: Lib Dem MP quits frontbench job over Ed Davey's leadership
summary: Deputy party leader Daisy Cooper says "the vast majority of our MPs support Ed... and are furious at this distraction."
body:
Sir Ed Davey and Charlie Maynard on the campaign trail in 2024
Liberal Democrat MP Charlie Maynard has resigned from the party's frontbench and wants to see Sir Ed Davey replaced as leader.
Asfirst reported by the Financial Times,external, the Witney MP left his role as Treasury spokesman on Friday.
Those close to Sir Ed privately acknowledge that there is what they see as a "small group" of Liberal Democrat MPs who are not happy with his leadership, of which Maynard is one.
Daisy Cooper, the deputy leader of the party, said: "The vast majority of our MPs support Ed, want him to lead the party into the next election, and are furious at this distraction." The BBC has approached Maynard for comment.
Lib Dem MP and former leader Tim Farron also defended Sir Ed, saying under his leadership the party was in a position to match or even beat the "record numbers of MPs" the party won at the last election.
"To think we're helped by this kind of rubbish, you'd need to be smoking the kind of stuff even we aren't in favour of legalising," he quipped.
Several other Lib Dem MPs, including some frontbenchers, also gave Davey their backing in social media posts on Friday evening.
Julian Brazil, a Liberal Democrat council leaderwho has previously been critical of Sir Ed,said Maynard had "put his head above the parapet - we'll see if other people follow".
Speaking to BBC Radio 5Live's Matt Chorley, he said: "I would have thought that in the next few days, we will see if there's a groundswell behind him."
Brazil added that Sir Ed had been a "fantastic leader" but added: "For whatever reasons people aren't listening to Ed, they don't take notice of him, so we need to have a fresh start and be able to articulate what our vision of the country is.
"I think that's best done by someone else."
Maynard was first elected to his Oxfordshire constituency in 2024, winning the traditionally Conservative seat, formerly held by David Cameron, with a majority of more than 4,000.
Before becoming an MP, he ran an international mergers and acquisitions advisory firm.
He is the second Lib Dem to leave the frontbench this week, following Alison Bennett's decision to resign her post of spokesperson for care and carers.
Bennett would not confirmed why she stepped down but it is understood it was not for personal reasons.
Under Liberal Democrat rules, a leadership contest can be triggered if a vote of no confidence in the leader is passed by the majority of all the party's MPs.
To enter a leadership contest, a Lib Dem MP must have nominations from at least 10% of the parliamentary party, not including the candidate themselves, and have the backing of 200 members across at least 20 local parties.
Sir Ed has been leader for six years and in the 2024 general election led the party to its biggest election success, winning 72 seats.
However, the party has found it difficult to build on that success, with polling numbers remaining at relatively low levels.
More recently, some Liberal Democrats have publicly attacked the leader for his stance on the triple lock - the mechanism which guarantees the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases, or 2.5% whichever is highest.
Last week, Sir Ed criticised Andy Burnham's announcement that he would adjust the triple lock, arguing it would "put more pensioners into poverty".
"This would mean people who are working hard now - the millennials - when they retire would have a very poor pension," he said.
One Lib Dem MP described Sir Ed's argument as "nonsense", while another said: "Most millennials don't think there will be a state pension when they retire so this isn't being done with them in mind."

title: Polanski vows to stay as Green leader as he faces criticism after by-election defeat
summary: Jewish Greens' leader has said Polanski should resign in the wake of a Zionism row and by-election defeat.
body:
Polanski was challenged on Radio 4's Today over whether he thinks Israel has a right to exist
Zack Polanski has vowed to stay on as Green Party leader after his by-election defeat, as he faced pressure from within his own party to resign.
The leader of the Jewish Greens, Vivien Lichtenstein, said on Friday he should resign, adding it was a "big mistake" for him to have dodged a debate about a party conference motion that declared Zionism a form of racism.
Lichtenstein's comments come after two former Green leaders accused Polanski of failing to show leadership over the Zionism row.
Polanski, whocame second to Labourovernight in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, told BBC Breakfast he would "absolutely" stay on as leader and he "of course" had not questioned that.
The Greens had hoped to take the seat, previously held by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, after aby-election success earlier this year.
Polanski lost out in Thursday's contest in London to Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali - who secured 45% of the vote to his 33% - but the Green vote share was up by 22 percentage points on the 2024 general election.
Following the by-election, Lichtenstein was asked whether it would be right for Polanski to continue as leader of the party. She told Times Radio: "No, I think he should resign."
Earlier in the week, Lichtenstein, who has been a member of the Green Party for nearly three decades, told Radio 4's Today programme it was "quite possible" she would leave the party after the Zionism row.
Speaking to the BBC's Victoria Derbyshire on Friday, she said she would not resign immediately because she is having conversations about how to "detoxify" the party.
When asked if she had confidence in Polanski's leadership, Lichtenstein said: "At the moment, no I don't." She added that she was "very disappointed" in him.
Calling on Polanski to apologise, she said: "I don't think that any Jew in the party is going to be in any danger...
"There just might be some unpleasant people who will direct some unpleasant comments, and some of us are going to have to deal with them robustly."
Her criticisms were similar to those of former Green Party leader Caroline Lucas who said Polanski should have attended the vote on the conference motion on Sunday.
The motion, which was passed by rank-and-file members to become official party policy, defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backed a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.
Adrian Ramsay, a Green MP and former co-leader, declined to back Polanski on Friday, and said he was now working to reverse the motion.
"A lot depends on what happens in the days and weeks to come," he told the BBC's Politics East, when asked if Polanski should still lead the party.
"[He] did not show leadership I would have been looking for."
Ellie Chowns, the Green MP for North Herefordshire, said she "unequivocally" backs Israel's right to exist and is "passionately opposed to the actions of the current Israeli government under Netanyahu".
"I believe it's for both Israelis and Palestinians themselves to decide what the ultimate constitutional settlement should look like in their region," she told BBC News.
"I believe both Israel and Palestine have the right to exist.
"I believe that's a perspective shared by the large majority of Green Party members and by the large majority of the British people."
Polanski defended his absence from the controversial motion vote in Brighton, saying he was busy campaigning in the North London constituency.
Asked if he would resign, he said: "Of course I can carry on as leader of the Green Party.
"Yes, I've taken a loss tonight but our movement is so much bigger than one election or one motion."
Having not answered questions about the Zionism vote for most of this week, Polanski confirmed in interviews on Friday that he would nothave voted for the "imperfect" motion without it being amended.
However, he said "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by a racist ideology".
Several UN reports have accused the Israeli government of committing war crimes which amount to genocide in Gaza. Israel has repeatedly denied all such allegations.
On Friday morning, following the Zionism row, Polanski was asked repeatedly on BBC Radio 4's Today programme whether he believes Israel has a right to exist.
"I don't believe any state has the right to oppress or to commit apartheid and certainly not genocide on another people," he said, adding: "I don't believe that's a state that anyone should be supporting."
Asked by presenter Nick Robinson for a "yes/no" answer on this question, he said: "I've repeated many times that I want to see equal rights for Israelis and Palestinians - at the moment Palestinians don't have equal rights so I think I'm answering your question really clearly."
In private, plenty of longstanding Green figures remain frustrated and accuse Polanski of being "missing in action" over the motion.
They say the result is an untenable situation where he leads a party whose policy on the Middle East he disagrees with.
"He is in danger of losing the confidence of both wings," one critic pointed out, referring to how some supporters of the motion have now been left irritated too by Polanski's refusal to publicly back them.

Labour sees off Green challenge to win Holborn by-election
But given his popularity among the grassroots, he may be safe from a leadership challenge in the near future.
Former Green leader Caroline Lucas described the motion as "dangerous" and "flawed from top to bottom", and said leadership "was frankly missing" on it.
She said she was not calling for Polanski to stand down and welcomed that he had "indicated he shares some of my concerns on the Zionism motion".
"Now the party needs to come together to make the urgent changes needed to take us forward," she said.
Jonathan Bartley, the Green co-leader from 2016 to 2021, called on Polanski to "put his hands up" and "say sorry" - but did not demand he quit.
"I think [the vote] was a failure of leadership from Zack and there is a certain toxicity now around the Green Party," he told BBC Radio 4's World at One.
Bartley said the Green brand "needs to be detoxified", adding the party had seen an influx in members that have "maybe come from the left of the Labour Party, maybe from [Jeremy Corbyn's] Your Party" but "we're losing some older voters".
The party's next scheduled leadership ballot takes place in summer 2027, and Bartley said he thinks Polanski will face a challenger.
Siân Berry, Green MP for Brighton Pavilion, said on Friday she was ready to work with colleagues "to restore trust in our processes and our party, fix the serious flaws in the motion that was passed" and build more inclusive policies.
The Green leader has faceddays of pressureover the Zionism motion. Four of the five Green MPs and one of the party's two deputy leaders opposed it, the Green deputy in Wales and some councillors resigned, while some local members and the European Green Party have distanced themselves from it.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called on Polanski to reverse the "completely wrong" motion.
Meanwhile, Labour chair Bridget Phillipson drew comparisons withher party's previous antisemitism scandal, telling the BBC she felt the Greens now face a "serious problem" with antisemitism.
Polanski has said anti-Zionism and antisemitism are distinct from each other and saidnobody will be excludedfrom the party on the basis of their faith, place of worship or religious body.
